'''Michael Levine''' is an American [[Developmental biology|developmental]] and [[cell biologist]] at [[Princeton University]], where he is the director of the Lewis-Sigler Institute for Integrative Genomics and a Professor of Molecular Biology.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://molbio.princeton.edu/faculty/molbio-faculty/891-levine|title=Molecular Biology Faculty Michael Levine}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://lsi.princeton.edu/about/lsi-history|title=LSI History}}</ref>

Levine previously held appointments at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], the [[University of California, San Diego]], and [[Columbia University]]. He is notable for co-discovering the [[homeobox]] in 1983 and for discovering the organization of the regulatory regions of developmental genes.<ref name="firefly">{{cite journal |first1=Karen |last1=Hopkin |url=http://classic.the-scientist.com/article/home/52885/ |title=Fire Fly |journal=The Scientist |volume=21 |issue=3 |page=58 |date=March 1, 2007}}</ref>

==Biography==
Levine was born in [[West Hollywood]] and raised in [[Los Angeles]]<ref name="firefly" /> in [[United States|America]].  Levine studied biology as an undergraduate at [[UC Berkeley]], studying biology with [[Allan Wilson (biologist)|Allan Wilson]]<ref name="firefly" /> and graduating in 1976.<ref name="UCSD-PR">[http://libraries.ucsd.edu/historyofucsd/newsreleases/1996/19960430b.html UCSD Press Release], April 30, 1996.</ref> He went on to graduate studies at [[Yale]], where he studied with [[Alan Garen]] and in 1981 received a Ph.D. in [[molecular biophysics]] and [[biochemistry]].<ref name="UCSD-PR" />

Levine joined the Princeton faculty in 2015, and had been a professor at [[UC Berkeley]] after leaving UCSD in 1996.<ref name="wilburcross">[http://www.aya.yale.edu/content/2009-winners-bios Wilbur Cross Medal 2009 Winners Bios], [[Yale University]] (last visited 2012 July 29) ("The [[Wilbur Lucius Cross Medal]] is an honor presented each year by the Graduate School Alumni Association to a small number of outstanding alumni. The medal recognizes distinguished achievements in scholarship, teaching, academic administration, and public service–all areas in which the legendary Dean Cross excelled.")</ref>
[[File:Drosophila_melanogaster_Proboscis.jpg|right|thumb|200x200px|''Drosophila Melanogaster'', the object of Levine's science]]

=== Discoveries ===
==== Homeobox ====
Levine was a post-doc with [[Walter Gehring]] in Switzerland from 1982 to 1983.<ref name="scimusuk">[http://www.sciencemuseum.org.uk/WhoAmI/FindOutMore/Yourbody/Howdoyoubecomeyou/Howdoestheembryodevelop/Howisthebodyshaped.aspx "What have you got in common with a fly?"], Science Museum, South Kensington, UK (last visited July 29, 2012).</ref>  There, he co-discovered the [[homeobox]] with Ernst Hafen and fellow post-doc [[William McGinnis]]:<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/308428a0 |title=A conserved DNA sequence in homoeotic genes of the Drosophila Antennapedia and bithorax complexes |year=1984 |last1=McGinnis |first1=W. |last2=Levine |first2=M. S. |last3=Hafen |first3=E. |last4=Kuroiwa |first4=A. |last5=Gehring |first5=W. J. |journal=Nature |volume=308 |issue=5958 |pages=428–33 |pmid=6323992|bibcode = 1984Natur.308..428M |s2cid=4235713 }}
</ref>
<blockquote>After learning that [[Ultrabithorax]], a gene that specifies the development of wings, showed a localized pattern of expression similar to that of [[Antennapedia]], they decided to revisit the classic papers of [[Edward B. Lewis|Ed Lewis]]. In 1978, Lewis had proposed that all these [[homeotic gene]]s (the ones that tell animals where to put a wing and where to put a leg and so on) arose from a common ancestral gene. So McGinnis carved up the Antennapedia gene and, using those pieces as probes, the trio identified eight genes, which turned out to be the eight homeotic genes in flies. "That pissed off a lot of people," says Levine. "The homeotic genes were the trophies of the [[Drosophila genome|''Drosophila'' genome]]. And we got 'em all. I mean, we got 'em all!" Far from being humble, Levine says, "We were like, 'We kicked your ass pretty good, didn't we, baby!' Those were the days."<ref name="firefly" /></blockquote>

==== ''eve'' stripe 2 enhancer ====
Levine briefly returned to [[UC Berkeley]] as a postdoctoral fellow<ref name="UCSD-PR" /> with [[Gerry Rubin]].<ref name="currbio">[http://www.cell.com/current-biology/retrieve/pii/S0960982203004664 Mike Levine (Abstract)], ''[[Current Biology]]'', v.13, n.14, R545 (July 15, 2003).</ref>  He then joined the faculty of [[Columbia University]], where he "led the discovery of the modular organization of the regulatory regions of developmental genes."<ref name="firefly-carroll" />  After isolating the ''even-skipped'' (''eve'') gene, Levine's team determined that each of the seven stripes was produced by separate enhancers.<ref name="firefly" />  With further study they discovered that both a set of activators and a set of [[repressors]] worked together to shape the expression of ''eve'' in the second stripe, and determined that the repressors shut down only their binding enhancers, leaving other enhancers free of repression.<ref name="firefly" /> Joseph Corbo said of the work, <blockquote>"Before Levine's studies of even-skipped stripe 2, it wasn't clear how you generated spatially restricted patterns of gene expression from initially broad crude gradients of morphogens.  I think that the even-skipped stripe 2 studies were the defining studies that showed how an organism can interpret those gradients and turn them into specific patterns of gene expression. To me that's Mike's crowning achievement."<ref name="firefly" /></blockquote>

==== Ascidian ''Ciona'' ====
After earning tenure in only four years at Columbia,<ref name="firefly" /> Levine moved to [[UCSD]] in 1991,<ref name="UCSD-PR" /> where he added the [[sea squirt]], ''[[Ciona intestinalis]]'', to his repertoire.  Much of Levine's work, including his homeobox studies, has been done in ''[[Drosophila]]''.<ref name="scimusuk" /> Levine's team is also prominent in work with the [[sea squirt]], ''[[Ciona intestinalis]]'', an invertebrate that facilitates study of development.<ref name="firefly" /> For example, this work included insights into classical myodeterminants<ref name="spikes">{{cite book |doi=10.1007/978-4-431-66982-1_30 |chapter=''Ci-sna cis''-Regulation of Ascidian Tail Muscle Genes |title=The Biology of Ascidians |year=2001 |last1=Erives |first1=Albert |last2=Levine |first2=Michael |isbn=978-4-431-66984-5 |pages=193–201}}</ref><ref name="spike2">{{cite journal |doi=10.1006/dbio.2000.9815 |title=Characterization of a Maternal T-box Gene in Ciona intestinalis |year=2000 |last1=Erives |first1=Albert |last2=Levine |first2=Michael |journal=Developmental Biology |volume=225 |pages=169–78 |pmid=10964472 |issue=1|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="spike1">{{cite journal |doi=10.1006/dbio.1997.8810 |title=Lineage-Specific Regulation of the ''Ciona snail'' Gene in the Embryonic Mesoderm and Neuroectoderm |year=1998 |last1=Erives |first1=Albert |last2=Corbo |first2=Joseph C. |last3=Levine |first3=Michael |journal=Developmental Biology |volume=194 |issue=2 |pages=213–25 |pmid=9501022|doi-access=free }}</ref> and the composition of the [[notochord]], the defining tissue of the [[chordate phylum]].<ref name="spikex">{{cite journal |doi=10.1101/gad.13.12.1519 |title=Brachyury downstream notochord differentiation in the ascidian embryo |year=1999 |last1=Takahashi |first1=H. |last2=Hotta |first2=K. |last3=Erives |first3=A. |last4=Di Gregorio |first4=A. |last5=Zeller |first5=R. W. |last6=Levine |first6=M. |last7=Satoh |first7=N. |journal=Genes & Development |volume=13 |issue=12 |pages=1519–23 |pmid=10385620 |pmc=316807}}</ref>

=== Awards ===
* 1982 – [[Jane Coffin Childs Postdoctoral Fellowship]]<ref name="currbio" />
* 1985 – [[Searle Scholars Research Fellowship]]<ref>[http://www.searlescholars.net/person/375 "Michael Levine"], Searle Scholars Program directory. (last visited July 29, 2012).</ref>
* 1985 – [[Alfred P. Sloan Fellowship]]<ref>[https://www.nytimes.com/1985/03/10/nyregion/90-scientists-and-economists-win-sloan-research-awards.html "90 Scientists and Economists Win Sloan Research Awards"], ''[[New York Times]]'', March 10, 1985.</ref>
* 1996 – [[NAS Award in Molecular Biology]] - "For his insightful contributions to our understanding of gene regulation networks and molecular mechanisms governing the development of organisms with a segmented body plan."<ref>[http://nas.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_molbio "NAS Award in Molecular Biology"] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120722011217/http://nas.nasonline.org/site/PageServer?pagename=AWARDS_molbio |date=2012-07-22 }}, National Academy of Sciences (Awarded for recent notable discovery in molecular biology by a young scientist age 45 or younger).</ref>
* 1998 - Elected to [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in "Cellular and Developmental Biology" section: "Utilizing an elegant blend of in vitro and in vivo studies, Levine carried out insightful and complete analysis of regulatory events that govern segmentation and dorsal-ventral polarity in Drosophila. His work provided a dramatic example of combinatorial regulation at a complex enhancer and established new paradigms for transcriptional control."<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20160304035840/http://nas.nasonline.org/site/Dir/2083705746?pg=vprof&mbr=1001182&returl=http://nas.nasonline.org/site/Dir/2083705746?pg%3Dsrch%26view%3Dbasic&retmk=search_again_link "Michael S. Levine"], National Academy of Sciences Member Directory (last visited 2012 July 29).</ref>
* 2009 – [[Wilbur Cross Medal]] (Yale Alumni Association)<ref name="wilburcross" />
* 2015 – Edwin G. Conklin Medal from the [[Society for Developmental Biology]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Levine_Conklin Medal |url=https://www.sdbonline.org/sites/SDBe-news/Fall2015/Levine_Conklin.html |access-date=2026-05-22 |website=www.sdbonline.org}}</ref>

=== Professional relations ===
Levine cites as a significant influence his instructor Fred Wilt (taking his developmental biology class "was probably the single most galvanizing experience I had in terms of defining my future goals"),<ref name="currbio" /> and cites fellow scientists [[Eric H. Davidson|Eric Davidson]], [[Peter Lawrence (biologist)|Peter Lawrence]] and [[Christiane Nusslein-Volhard]] as "mentors [and] friends ... over the years".<ref name="currbio"/>

On choosing to become a research biologist, he described some family pressure to become a doctor ("Coming from a modest background, particularly a Jewish family, the pressure to become a doctor was intense"),<ref name="firefly" />

Fellow biologist [[Sean B. Carroll|Sean Carroll]] said of Levine, "Mike's work has done for animal development what the work on the [[lac operon]] and [[phage lambda]] did for understanding [[gene regulation]] in simpler organisms ... [Those] two big discoveries had a very large conceptual significance for [[developmental biology]] and by extension for [[evolutionary biology]]."<ref name="firefly-carroll">[[Sean B. Carroll]], quoted in {{cite journal |first1=Karen |last1=Hopkin |url=http://classic.the-scientist.com/article/home/52885/ |title=Fire Fly |journal=The Scientist |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=58 |date=March 1, 2007}}</ref>
